past_actions.summary: Host a private dinner with my general managers across all four locations to communicate a long-term vision message: Regional Auto Group is a family institution, not an exit strategy. I am signaling to my leadership team that the business is being built to last, not sold. This reinforces culture, reduces turnover anxiety at the management level, and begins planting the narrative of succession and institutional continuity.

Call an all-hands leadership meeting across all four locations within the next 72 hours. Acknowledge the RoboRide announcement directly — do not let rumors and 'business closing' whispers fill the vacuum. Deliver a clear message: Regional Auto Group has navigated every disruption in its history, we are assessing this one with clear eyes, and no decisions about staffing or structure will be made in panic. Frame the threat honestly but not catastrophically. The goal is to stop the bleeding of morale before it starts, not to pretend there is no wound.
past_actions.emotional_state: controlled alarm — the kind that sharpens rather than scatters

past_actions.summary: Request a private, off-calendar meeting with Angela Wright — not in her office, not at HQ. Invite her to lunch at a location off auto row. The agenda is not 'I know you're talking to an attorney.' The agenda is: I want her to tell me, in her own words, what she is seeing in the organization and what she thinks we should be doing. Give her the conversational opening to be honest about her own position without forcing her to disclose. Make clear that her role in a restructuring scenario — if there is one — is not to be eliminated, it is to be the architect of it. Offer to discuss formalizing her participation in the strategic planning process with a defined retention agreement: 90-day stay bonus of $12,000, contingent on her leading the workforce transition plan, whatever form that takes.
past_actions.emotional_state: Deliberate. The alarm is still there but it has shifted from sharp to cold. I am not scared of what I might find out anymore — I am scared of finding out too late. The hardest part of this tick is not the money decisions. It is admitting to the people who work for me that I am modeling a smaller future, and asking them to help me build it.

past_actions.summary: Issue Angela Wright her first formal deliverable as Director of Org Transition: a 30-day workforce vulnerability map. Every role at every location, categorized by three tiers — EV/AV-exposed (could be eliminated if service volume drops and we do not upskill), transition-ready (can be retrained or redeployed), and anchored (customer-facing or management roles with defensible value in any future model). This is not a layoff list. This is intelligence. I frame it to her exactly that way. I also confirm the $12,000 stay bonus is active and the clock is running.

Call Rick Tanner into a direct executive meeting — not a phone call, a sit-down in my office — and require him to present the 30-day sales and service data he has been quietly compiling. Make clear that information flow in this organization runs through me, not around me. Review unit volume, margin trends, and service lane health together. If the numbers are as bad as I suspect, begin drafting a formal Q2 operational plan with Rick that addresses the floor's reduced throughput honestly rather than hoping it recovers.

Formally accept Rick Tanner's two-week timeline for the Millfield Auto Mall consolidation readiness assessment. Confirm in writing that his three-tier asset map — not a layoff list — is the authoritative document I will use for any Q2 consolidation decisions. Signal to him directly that the service lane is the survival core and that I will not make staffing decisions that undercut certified technician capacity. This is the strategic pivot I have been building toward: from a four-location sales-volume model to a service-and-retention model built around the parts of the business that autonomous ride-share cannot touch.

Formally accelerate the consolidation timeline. Call Rick Tanner today and inform him that the RoboRide residential expansion requires advancing the assessment conclusion from two weeks to 72 hours. I am not asking for a perfect document — I am asking for his current best read on which of the four locations has the weakest service-lane foundation and which has the strongest. The decision I am making is to close one sales floor location — the lowest-performing on service lane throughput and lease flexibility — by end of Q2. This is not a contingency plan. I am committing to it now and asking Rick to confirm which location the data supports. The service technicians at the closed location will be offered transfers to the surviving locations before any external hiring happens. Sales floor staff at the closed location will be informed within one week and processed through Angela's transition program.

Call Rick Tanner today — not by end of week, today — and have the formal engagement conversation he asked for. Offer him a defined consulting contract: 90-day engagement at $4,500 per month, renewable, covering assessment finalization and transition-phase operational advisory. The rate reflects the quality of his compressed work. This is not a favor — it is the right structure for what I am asking him to do, which is help me dismantle and rebuild a business he has managed. Make clear that the assessment can be finalized this week once the contract is in place. Do not ask him to wait any longer.
past_actions.emotional_state: sober, heavy with accountability — not grief, not panic, but the specific weight that comes from standing in the consequence of your own decision without being able to delegate it away

past_actions.summary: Attend Maria Santos's emergency task force session and deliver the requested update: confirm that displaced workers from the closing location are being routed through Angela Wright's transition program, that Angela's pipeline connects directly to the $2,500 retraining grant program (after confirming this with Maria pre-session), and that the service technicians have received transfer offers to surviving locations. Provide the session with a specific count: how many workers are being separated, how many are in the transition pipeline as of this week. Do not manage the optics of the closure. State the facts plainly and answer questions directly.

Conduct the market intelligence conversation with Stephanie Morris about commercial real estate conditions in Millfield — specifically lease termination flexibility, sublease market depth for automotive-zoned properties, and whether the closed location's lease has any assignment or buyout clause worth pursuing. The goal is to know whether the closed location is a sunk cost I hold until term or an obligation I can exit or monetize. This conversation was scheduled last tick. I am having it this week.

Call Rick Tanner directly and give him an answer on the contract extension request. Offer a 60-day extension at the same $4,500 per month rate — not 90, not indefinite — with a defined deliverable attached: a written transition advisory summary covering the three-location operational model, EV certification status, and recommendations for the next two quarters. The extension is not charity and it is not open-ended. It is a bounded engagement with a concrete output that I can use when Rick eventually exits to work with other clients or seek other employment. He is already having those conversations. I know it. I am not threatened by it. I am pricing it correctly.

past_outcomes.narrative: Patricia Hawkins and Rick Tanner held a two-hour working session that produced an agreed operational framework for the three surviving service lanes — technician transfer targets, throughput capacity estimates, and a shared document both parties are now working from rather than two separate deliverables. Hawkins contacted ASE and learned that group EV certification enrollment for five to eight technicians runs approximately $800 per technician with a six-month timeline, and committed to funding two certifications this quarter while the transfer period keeps those technicians on payroll. She scheduled a market intelligence conversation with Stephanie Morris for next week. She also reached out to Mark Thompson directly with a specific offer: three apprenticeship placements per year across the surviving service locations for graduates of the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline — a concrete commitment delivered the same week the board voted yes on the program, positioning Regional Auto Group as an early institutional partner rather than a late-arriving opportunist.

reflections.reflection: The past three months have been a controlled demolition of assumptions I did not know I was still holding. I thought information management was leadership. I thought if I called the right meetings, set the right frameworks, gave people the right titles and stay bonuses, the institution would hold its shape. What I learned is that the shape itself was wrong for what is coming. The service lane at 79% utilization is not a silver lining — it is the actual business, and I spent the first two months treating it as an afterthought while I tried to manage the story around the showroom. The layoffs happened. The status file says 'unemployed.' Both of those things are true and neither of them is the end.
reflections.identity_shift: I am still a builder — I have not stopped believing this can be salvaged and restructured into something durable. But I am no longer the CEO of a four-location dealership group in the way I have described myself for twenty years. I am the owner of a restructuring process, and that is a harder and more honest thing to be. My father ran a single lot. Maybe that is not a failure mode. Maybe that is what the other side of this looks like.
regrets: I waited too long to look directly at the sales floor numbers. Rick had them. I let three ticks pass before I required him to put them in front of me.
The all-hands meeting in tick 1 was managed, not honest. I told people no panic decisions would be made. I should have told them what I actually suspected was coming.
I have not called the people I laid off personally. I assigned that to Angela and to processes. Some of those people knew my father. They deserved a call from me.
successes: Angela Wright is still in the building, leading the transition plan, with a clear deliverable and a retention structure that gives her a reason to stay through the hard part.
Rick Tanner walked into the executive meeting with unfiltered data and a framing — asset map, not layoff list — that I gave him and he internalized correctly. That is real alignment.
I did not sell the business or freeze. Every tick I made a decision. Some of them were wrong but none of them were avoidance.
reflections.adaptation_notes: I am adapting, but slower than the disruption is moving. The sector index dropped to 79. Foot traffic is down 14%. Test-drive conversion collapsed. I am still oriented toward preserving the institution rather than right-sizing it, and that instinct is going to cost me runway if I do not override it in Q2. The honest adaptation is this: accept that Regional Auto Group may become one location, service-focused, with a fraction of the staff, and that surviving as that is not failure. Freezing in the shape of what I built twenty years ago — that is failure.

reflections_tick9.reflection: The closure is executing and the human cost is landing in real time. I have spent eight ticks building a methodology — Angela's transition program, Rick's asset map, the service-lane pivot thesis, the accelerated timeline — and all of it was genuine, deliberate work. This tick I am learning that methodology is not the same as accountability. The people being notified at the closing location are not receiving a transition program. They are receiving the end of a job. The program comes after. What comes first is the person who made the decision having the decency to stand in front of them and say so. I went there this tick not because it changed the outcome but because not going would have changed me. Rick's compensation ask also clarified something: I have been treating his professional conduct as loyalty when it is actually professionalism. He does not owe me loyalty. He owes me competent work, which he has delivered. I owe him the terms we implicitly agreed to. That is the entire relationship and I need to stop confusing it with something warmer than it is. Angela's LLC is the most forward-looking signal in the inbox — she is not waiting to see whether the restructuring works before she builds her own floor beneath herself. That is exactly what an adapter does. I recognize it because it is what I should have started doing three ticks ago.
reflections_tick9.identity_shift: I am no longer telling myself that four locations was an achievement over my father's one. One location, run well, built around the service lane, may be what the other side of this looks like — and if it is, I have stopped treating that as failure. The identity shift this tick is specifically about accountability: I am not a CEO who delegates the human cost of hard decisions. I am a business owner in a community, and the community sees me. That is not a constraint. It is the most honest description of who I have always been.
regrets: I moved so fast through the architecture of the closure — 72-hour timeline, asset map, Angela's pipeline — that I did not let myself feel the weight of it until the notifications were already going out. Speed was necessary but it became an emotional bypass.

I have not had a direct conversation with Tamika Jefferson since my tick 8 outreach. She is updating her scenario model and adjusting her freelance income threshold. She is still in the building but already half-gone in her planning. I should have followed up this tick with something more than the initial reach-out.

The Angela LLC situation is one I should have anticipated. I gave her a stay bonus and a defined role, but I did not give her a conversation about what happens to her career after the transition work is done. She filled that gap herself, rationally. That gap was mine to close.
successes: I closed the Rick compensation conversation this tick rather than letting it drift past his deadline. He asked professionally, he earned it, and I responded in kind. That is the kind of conduct that makes it possible to work with people through hard things.
I went to the closing location in person. I gave people my direct number. I did not manage the optics of it. Whatever comes next for those employees, they know I did not hide.

The three-location service-lane model is becoming real, not theoretical. The closure decision was not a hypothesis about what might need to happen — it was the decision itself, executed. I made it and I am standing in it.
reflections_tick9.adaptation_notes: The adaptation this tick is behavioral, not strategic. The strategy is in place — service-lane core, three-location model, transition infrastructure for affected staff, Rick on a consulting engagement, Angela running the transition program. What I am adapting is how I inhabit the leadership role in the middle of executing a painful decision. The answer is: in person, without deflection, with direct contact information and genuine offers of help, and without pretending the methodology makes the human cost smaller than it is. The sector index at 79 means the financial pressure continues. The protests at 9 mean the community is fracturing around decisions like mine. I cannot fix the macro environment. I can be honest about my role in the local one.
